tip: भाई (bhai = brother) attaches to any man's name as friendly respect – कमल भाई (Kamal bhai) is not your sibling. Hindi lends family words to everyone.
आना (aana) is just the base 'to come' form, used here as a soft, friendly request – 'do come over'. It lands gentler than the bare command आ (aa).
तू (tu) is the most intimate of Hindi's three words for 'you' – close friends, kids, God. With a stranger it can insult. The safe default is आप (aap).
जी (ji) alone at the start of a reply means 'yes' or 'sure' – the same syllable that adds respect after a name. One tiny word, two polite jobs.
With ने (ne), the verb agrees with what was written, not the writer: रामचरितमानस (Ramcharitmanas) is treated as feminine, so लिखी (likhi) – even though Tulsidas is a man.
English makes a decision; Hindi takes one: फ़ैसला लिया (faisla liya = took a decision), with लेना (lena = to take) as the partner verb.
तक (tak) covers both 'by' and 'until'. शुक्रवार तक (shukravaar tak) is a deadline here – by Friday – but with an ongoing action the same तक reads as until. Context decides.
Hindi pairs its relatives: जिसने (jisne = whoever) must be answered by उसने (usne) in the second half. English drops the second pronoun – Hindi keeps both.
Hindi runs two word stocks side by side: ज़िंदगी (zindagi) is the Persian-side word, जीवन (jeevan) the Sanskrit-side one. Same meaning – zindagi sounds everyday, jeevan formal or literary.
No 'would have' word here – the -ती (-ti) ending alone marks the unreal past: न होती... बर्बाद हो जाती (na hoti... barbaad ho jaati) = hadn't rained... would have been ruined.
'The more... the more' is a matched pair in Hindi: जितना (jitna = as much) opens, उतना ही (utna hi = that much) closes. One without the other sounds unfinished.
थूककर चाटना (thook-kar chaatna) is literally 'to spit, then lick it back up' – Hindi's image for breaking your word: reclaiming something you already put out.
सूचित किया जाता है (soochit kiya jaata hai = it is informed) never names who is informing. This doer-less passive is the standard opener of official Hindi notices.
पर्दा उठते ही (parda uthte hi) = 'the instant the curtain rose'. Verb + ते ही (te hi) squeezes a whole 'as soon as' clause into the verb plus one tiny word.
The ना (na) after मत जाओ (mat jao = don't go) is not a 'no' – tacked onto a request it softens it, like 'come on, don't go'. मत (mat) alone does the forbidding.
पकाया जाता है (pakaya jata hai = is cooked) is built on जाना (jaana = to go): literally 'goes cooked'. Hindi's passive runs on 'go', not on 'is' like English.
यात्रियों से अनुरोध है (yatriyon se anurodh hai) is literally 'from passengers a request is' – Hindi requests point से (se = from) at the person being asked, not 'to' them.
टिकट काटा (tikat kaata) is literally 'cut a ticket' – काटना (kaatna = to cut) is the standard verb for issuing tickets, receipts, and fines, from tearing them off a pad.
पधारें (padharein) is an honorific 'come', used on invitations to mean 'grace us with a visit'. In everyday speech you would say आएँ (aayein) – पधारें signals ceremony.
घड़ी (ghadi) usually means watch or clock, but दुख की घड़ी (dukh ki ghadi) is 'hour of grief' – घड़ी also names a moment in time, like English 'hour' in 'darkest hour'.
बंद रहेगा (band rahega) is 'will stay closed', not 'will be closed' – for a state holding through the day, Hindi prefers रहना (rahna = to stay) over होना (hona = to be).
बैठकर (baithkar) = 'having sat' – where English says 'sitting on the swing', Hindi adds -कर (kar) to the first action: sit-then-want, all in one word.
देखा जा सकता है (dekha ja sakta hai) = 'it can be seen' – literally 'seen go can'. Hindi builds 'can be X-ed' with जाना (jana = go) after the main verb.
करवाए गए (karvaye gaye) = 'were gotten done' – the -वा- (va) inside the verb means someone else did it. करना (karna) = do, करवाना (karvana) = have someone do.
Requests come FROM people in Hindi: कर्मचारियों से अनुरोध है (karmchariyon se anurodh hai) = 'from the employees is a request' – से (se = from), not 'to'.
'Because of' follows its noun: त्योहार के कारण (tyohar ke kaaran) = 'festival because-of'. के कारण (ke kaaran) always comes after the reason, never before.
English needs 'It is expected that' – Hindi just says उम्मीद है कि (ummeed hai ki = hope is that). No dummy 'it': the noun उम्मीद (ummeed = hope) leads.
चोर की दाढ़ी में तिनका (chor ki daadhi mein tinka) = 'a straw in the thief's beard' – guilt betrays itself. The nervous thief checks his own beard first.
पी गई (pee gayi) is drink + go, but the cat didn't go anywhere – the added 'go' marks the milk as completely finished. Hindi pairs verbs like this to show an action is done.
जिसकी लाठी उसकी भैंस (jiski laathi uski bhains) is literally 'whose stick, his buffalo' – whoever holds the stick keeps the buffalo. That is Hindi's image for might is right.
